event: VXE-455 lost all four lift motors at about 80 ft AGL during the vertical climb on launch, nosed over and crashed, destroying the lift booms and nose.
failure_mode: loss of lift on all four motors during climb, with VTOL AP and XComm power reset after the fall
contributing: VTOL AP log missing about 24 s before the crash (suspected failing SD card)
FWAP log starts late and FDR only partly recovered
no GCS log or AAR from the customer

evidence.quote: On launch during vertical ascent all four lift motors turned off at 50-75ft AGL.
if I had to guess, I would say it was a task lock scenario that would have resulted in a WDT
Based on the observed forward motors giving out first, plus the FW AP showing a downward pitch as it starts to fall, is it possible a connector or harness failed?
No Watch Dog Events are reported in the XComm debug message log file (XCEVLOG.txt).
XCOMM, FW AP, VTOL AP, Lift ESCs all operated normally upon simple testing.
My conclusion is still that something went wrong during the climb, but no smoking guns to what that is.

team_root_cause: Inconclusive due to missing log data. Logs indicate a failed lift system during climb. The failure occurred ~81' AGL.
team_view_in_comments: This sounds like task lock, likely resolved in a more recent firmware update.

would_settle_it.file: GCS debug log (C:\ProgramData\GCS\XEVTOLGCS) from customer laptop
would_settle_it.what: whether a VTOL SAFE or cut command was issued and the link state as the aircraft fell
plots of motor commands, vtVbatt and vtIbatt and the event timeline
whether the card is failing, which would explain the missing 24 s of VTOL data
boom power connector or harness damage that predates the impact

reasoning: The logs show the lift system failing during the climb, but the VTOL AP log is missing the last 24 s and no GCS log was obtained. Engineers offered two different guesses (a VTOL AP task lock without a logged watchdog, or a boom power connector or harness), and the bench check of XCOMM, FW AP, VTOL AP and lift ESCs found nothing. The evidence does not get past the symptom of total lift loss.
notes: Jason noted the forward motors gave out first, but this cannot be mapped to motor numbers and the failure was of all four motors, so position is left empty. The RMA-184 engineering evaluation and shipping PDFs converted with no text. The team closed this as Bermuda Triangle after the customer aircraft was replaced under goodwill.

event: VXE-501 made an uncommanded excursion during VTOL landing, rolling and turning 90 degrees right and flying about 150 m from the landing point in high wind; no crash.
component: main wing (right wing stall) in high wind during VTOL landing
failure_mode: right wing stall at high angle of attack with wind over 20 kt, while VTOL control had spooled down near zero, causing an uncommanded roll and turn right
contributing: VTOL lift control spooled down near zero so rotors had little authority
FW helper aileron response lowered the right aileron, adding camber
control algorithms not tuned for high wind VTOL flight (FS2-1392)

evidence.quote: the air vehicle turns 90 degrees to the right and then flies in typical fixed wing fashion to a position about 150 meters from the target landing spot.
On second look, the right wing appears to have stalled leading to the hard roll to the right.
The evidence for this is the high windspeed at low groundspeed, greater than 20kt, combined with greater than 10 degree pitch angle leading to the main wing carrying most of the weight of the AV.
In this situation, the VTOL control spools down near zero.
@Cameron Chapman no severe weather conditions noted.

team_root_cause: The root cause of the excursion is complex. The AV has found itself in a situation in which most of the weight of the AV is carried by the main wing due to an apparently high AoA and high airspeed due to high prevailing winds, over 20kt estimated. At the time of the excursion, the AV had little control authority from the rotors, and some control authority, in roll, from the ailerons. The current hypothesis is that the right wing experienced stall due to flow separation from high relative angle of attack higher camber than the left wing, resulting in significant unintended roll right, leading t

would_settle_it.what: pitch, estimated AoA and wingtip AoA at the moment of the roll, to confirm the right wing exceeded stall angle
estimated wind, airspeed, aileron and lift motor commands through the excursion

reasoning: Log analysis shows the aircraft at high pitch with estimated wind over 20 kt, so the main wing carried most of the weight while the lift rotors spooled down near zero. The team reads the hard roll right as a right wing stall made worse by the right aileron deflecting down. This rests on estimated AoA and wind rather than a direct measurement, and is stated as a hypothesis, so it narrows to a high wind wing stall rather than determining it.
notes: The operator reported no severe weather, which conflicts with the over 20 kt wind estimated from the logs. An early finding that the FW helper roll loop was inverted was later withdrawn. FDR, video and plots are listed only, not converted.

contributing: possible LRF failure seen in FDR

Lower priority tasks being promoted and blocking higher priority tasks.

event: VXE376 with 300 series lift booms and drop payloads pitched forward on attempted takeoff, fell out of the stand and broke a lift prop; follow-up hovers showed noise and wobble from the left boom.
component: lift rotor blade mount (keyed mount between lift motor and rotor)
failure_mode: keyed blade mount installed in the wrong orientation with loose screws, giving blade misalignment, imbalance, wobble and loss of lift
contributing: booms reassembled after full teardown for composite trim without QC check
loose lift boom bolts
mount design allows misassembly (VXEP-215: design change required)
testing continued despite known anomalies
flashing center wing LED from VTOL FW dropper configuration (separate issue)

evidence.quote: Front left lift motor aligns in the opposite direction (blade facing forward)
All lift motors started but the aircraft just pitched forward and didn’t take off the ground
Correlating data with video evidence from incident would indicate an issue with front left motor (M1)
Keyed blade mount was not orientated for associated hole.
Screws were also not tight, possibly leading to wobble.
This was first RC hover and first flight on this set of lift booms after complete tear down for composite trim.

team_root_cause:
Front Left lift rotor mount (mount interface between lift rotor and motor) was incorrectly oriented likely resulting in blade imbalance and loss of lift. 
Flashing CW LED due to dropper config in VTOL FW.
reasoning: Log data show the AP commanding nearly full throttle on the front left motor (M1) with no roll correction, matching the forward and left pitch seen on video. Teardown found the front left keyed blade mount not oriented to its hole and the screws loose, while the motor itself tested normal on the bench. After the mount was corrected the RC pilot reported a stable hover.
notes: The slide names the front left motor as M1, matching the VXEP-272 convention. An earlier comment suggested a wrong jumper harness install, but the teardown finding superseded it. The flashing center wing (CW) LED was a separate VTOL FW dropper configuration issue. Logs and video are listed only.

event: VXE-497, back at SLO on RMA, could not fly at flight test due to poor GPS signal; replacing ribbon cables and the corroded GPS header did not help, replacing GPS board SN GPS-1-1249 fixed it.
failure_mode: poor GPS signal from the board; teardown found no corrosion under the RF shield, and backup coin cell BT1 low at 1.745 V (expected about 3 V) is a suspected but unconfirmed cause
contributing: questionable avionics box ribbon cables and corrosion on the Green AP GPS header (replaced, issue remained)

evidence.quote: That was all replaced but issue remained.
NCR 1928 was generated and we replaced GPS board SN GPS-1-1249. After GPS Board replacement the issue appears to be resolved.
No evident corrosion underneath shield. BT1 (the coincell battery) is low at 1.745V when it should be at ~3V.
If the coincell batt drops below the min voltage, which is about 1.4V, it would cause the timing reference for the receiver to go out of whack
GPS Board SN GPS-1-1348 installed and passed SCO Checkout. Ready for flight test.

would_settle_it.file: GPS-1-1249 retest with fresh coin cell and reflash
would_settle_it.what: whether the board regains normal GPS signal once BT1 is replaced and the receiver is reflashed
BT1 voltage reading and condition of the board under the RF shield

notes: The board-level swap is direct evidence; the coin cell theory conflicts with the engineer's own stated minimum. RMA-181 induction PDF converted with no text. The RMA was opened for an unrelated center wing ODU connector issue.

event: During review of the VXE 487 crash logs, repeated FWAP to XComm ap link faults were found; on the bench they recurred each time the GCS connected and were later traced to GCS mission simulation.
component: GCS (legacy VXE SUAV) mission simulation running on the UI thread
failure_mode: mission simulation blocks the single threaded GCS from sending uplink messages, so the FWAP times out after about 5 s and logs an ap link fault
contributing: FWAP declares link loss after about 5 s without qualifying uplink messages
GCSS-434 fix canceled, no work done

evidence.quote: Ok shake didn't do it, but as soon as I connected using the GCS I got it to happen
Firmware update on XComm and FW AP was successful, but did not resolve the ap link fault issue
GCS mission sim appears to be the root cause and has been confirmed to cause this issue.
The GCS is a single threaded application, and when the mission sim is run the uplink messages are not sent to the vehicle.
The UI thread is also used for vehicle comms, which causes link faults.

team_root_cause: GCS mission simulation prevents GCS from servicing uplink resulting in vehicle reported link timeouts.
reasoning: The link faults were reproduced on the bench simply by connecting the GCS, not by shaking the avionics, and persisted after a firmware update, pointing away from the ribbon cable. FS2-2332 traced the message to the FWAP 5 s link timer and showed the fault always follows a GCS mission update, and the team confirmed the single threaded GCS mission simulation stops uplink messages.
notes: This ticket covers the link fault finding, not the VXE-487 crash itself, which is VXEP-101 (center wing power connector). Related link fault aborts are in VXEP-608.
